extra.message: The /sayhi endpoint formats user-controlled input into a template string and passes it to render_template_string(). User input flows: request.form['name'] → name template variable → string formatting with % → render_template_string(). This allows Jinja2 template expression injection like {{config}}, {{''.__class__.__mro__}}, etc.
User passwords are stored in plaintext in the database. The User model's password field (line 26) stores the raw string from registration without any hashing (line 30).

The application uses session-based authentication (cookie-based) but has no CSRF protection middleware or tokens. All POST endpoints (/login, /register/, /evaluate, /lookup, /xml, /sayhi) are vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery. An attacker can trick an authenticated user into performing actions without their consent.

The user-supplied 'name' parameter is embedded directly into the HTML response via string formatting (%s) without any HTML escaping. An attacker can submit <script>alert(1)</script> as the name, and it will execute in the browser. This is in addition to the SSTI vulnerability at the same location.

The /sayhi endpoint embeds user input directly into a Jinja2 template via Python string formatting (%s), then passes the entire string to render_template_string(). This allows an attacker to inject Jinja2 template expressions like {{ config }} or {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[2].__subclasses__() }} to access Flask internals and potentially achieve RCE.

The Flask session cookie is configured without SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True. When the application is served over HTTPS (which it should be in production), the session cookie will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, making it vulnerable to network sniffing.

The Flask secret_key is hardcoded as a predictable string 'Harry Potter And The Deathly Hallows'. This key is used to cryptographically sign session cookies. An attacker who knows or can guess this key can forge arbitrary session cookies, impersonate any user, and bypass all authentication.

The application has no CSRF protection implemented on any forms (login, register). Combined with the hardcoded secret key, an attacker can forge requests to perform actions on behalf of authenticated users. The Flask session uses cookies, making CSRF attacks feasible.

The Flask application secret key is hardcoded as a well-known string 'Harry Potter And The Deathly Hallows'. This is a constant string from popular culture that could be guessed or looked up by an attacker.

The User model defines the password column as a plain db.String(80) with no hashing or encryption. Passwords are stored in cleartext in the database. Anyone with database read access (SQL injection, backup file, DBA) can retrieve all user passwords.
User passwords are stored in plaintext in the database. The User model's password column stores the password string as-is with no hashing.

User passwords are stored in the database without any hashing or salting. The User.__init__ method directly assigns the raw password string to self.password. The login handler (line 50) compares the raw password from the form directly against the stored plaintext.
The login endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to perform unlimited brute-force password guessing attempts.

The application uses cookie-based sessions for authentication but has no CSRF protection (no CSRF tokens, no SameSite cookie attribute enforcement, no Origin/Referer header checking). The /login, /register/, and /logout endpoints can be abused via cross-site request forgery — an attacker can trick a victim's browser into submitting requests that log them in to the attacker's account, register a new account, or log them out.

After successful authentication, the session ID is not regenerated. An attacker who obtains or sets a victim's session ID before login can continue using the same session ID after login to hijack the authenticated session.
After successful authentication, the session ID is not regenerated. This allows an attacker to potentially fixate a session ID and hijack the user's session after login.

The login handler compares passwords in cleartext by passing both username and password directly into the ORM query: User.query.filter_by(username=name, password=passw). This means the password is transmitted and compared as plaintext in the database query, and no hashing is used.

User passwords are stored and compared in plaintext. The User model stores password directly, and login queries compare the raw password: User.query.filter_by(username=name, password=passw). No password hashing is used.

The login handler sets session['logged_in'] = True after successful authentication but never calls session.regenerate() to rotate the session ID. An attacker can fixate a victim's session ID before login and hijack the session after authentication.
The /register/ endpoint has no rate limiting or CAPTCHA. An attacker can create unlimited user accounts programmatically, filling the database with spam accounts.
The registration endpoint has no rate limiting, allowing an attacker to create unlimited user accounts programmatically.
User passwords are stored in the database as plaintext without any hashing or encryption. The password is directly taken from request.form and saved to the User model.
The /dashboard route does not check if the user is authenticated (no session['logged_in'] check). Any unauthenticated user can access it.

The /dashboard route (which exposes links to all vulnerability endpoints) does not check if the user is authenticated. Unlike the / route (home) which checks session['logged_in'], anyone can access the dashboard without logging in.
The 404 error handler passes the entire error/exception object to the error template, which renders it directly. This can leak internal application details.
The /evaluate endpoint, which allows arbitrary code execution via eval(), has no authentication check — any unauthenticated user can access it and execute arbitrary Python code on the server.

The /evaluate endpoint, which allows arbitrary code execution via eval(), has no authentication requirement. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and execute arbitrary Python code on the server.

The /evaluate route renders the string result of eval() directly into the HTML response without any escaping. If an attacker provides input that evaluates to a string containing HTML/JavaScript, it will be executed in the victim's browser.
User-supplied input from the 'expression' form field is passed directly to Python's eval() function with no sanitization. This allows arbitrary Python code execution.
User-controlled input from the 'expression' form field is passed directly to Python's eval() function without any sanitization. This allows arbitrary Python code execution on the server.
The /lookup endpoint, which allows OS command injection via nslookup, has no authentication check — any unauthenticated user can execute arbitrary shell commands.
The /lookup endpoint, which allows command injection via shell execution, has no authentication requirement. Any unauthenticated user can execute arbitrary shell commands.

The lookup() function calls rp() which is not defined anywhere in the codebase. This will cause a NameError at runtime, making the endpoint non-functional. Additionally, the intended behavior (executing a shell command with user input) is a command injection vulnerability (reported separately).

User-supplied 'address' input is concatenated directly into a shell command string 'nslookup ' + address and passed to the rp() function (which presumably executes shell commands). The user can inject shell metacharacters.

The /lookup route renders the raw output of the shell command directly into HTML without escaping. The shell output (which could contain attacker-injected content or control characters) is rendered in the browser.
The /xml endpoint, which allows XXE attacks, has no authentication check — any unauthenticated user can exploit XXE to read server files or perform SSRF.
The /xml endpoint, which allows XXE attacks via XML parsing, has no authentication requirement. Any unauthenticated user can submit malicious XML to read files or perform SSRF.

The XML parser is configured with no_network=False and dtd_validation=True, which allows external entity resolution and network access. User-supplied XML is parsed without disabling external entities.

The parsed XML content (which could contain attacker-controlled data via XXE) is directly concatenated into the HTML response without escaping. If the XML contains HTML/JavaScript, it will be rendered in the browser.
The /sayhi endpoint, which allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), has no authentication check — any unauthenticated user can achieve remote code execution via Jinja2 template injection.
The /sayhi endpoint, which allows SSTI attacks, has no authentication requirement. Any unauthenticated user can submit Jinja2 template expressions to achieve RCE.

User-supplied 'name' input is embedded directly into a Jinja2 template string via Python string formatting (%s), then rendered with render_template_string(). This allows the user to inject Jinja2 template expressions like {{ config }} or {{ ''.__class__.__mro__ }}.

The /sayhi route embeds user input directly into the HTML template string using Python string formatting before passing it to render_template_string. Since the user input is part of the static HTML (not inside a {{ }} expression), Jinja2's auto-escaping does NOT apply to it. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript.

The /sayhi endpoint takes user input via the 'name' form field, embeds it into a template string via Python string formatting (line 189, 204), then renders it with render_template_string() (line 205). User input containing Jinja2 template syntax (e.g., {{ config }}, {{ ''.__class__ }}) will be executed by the template engine, enabling SSTI.
Flask debug mode is enabled (app.debug = True) in the production configuration. This enables the Werkzeug debugger and interactive debugger console.
The Flask application is configured to listen on 0.0.0.0, binding to all available network interfaces including public-facing ones.

The 404 error handler passes the full error object to the template, which renders it directly via {{ error }}. Combined with app.debug = True, this exposes detailed error information including stack traces, source code snippets, and local variables to users.
The 404 error handler passes the exception object to the error template, which renders it via {{ error }}. This can leak internal server information including request paths and exception details.
The full error/exception object is rendered directly in the error template via {{ error }}. This exposes internal error details, stack traces, and potentially sensitive server information to users.
